title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion – or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?

paper.title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion – or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14 × 14\times and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607 × 1607\times , with marginal performance differences.

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Croitoru et al., 2023 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2021a ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) have consistently demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image synthesis in recent years. Some of the recent developments of diffusion models have focused on improving the quality of the generated samples. This is often achieved by a specialized post-training or fine-tuning phase ( Zhang et al., 2024c ; Luo et al., 2025 ) designed to improve the base models toward better visual and semantic results. This refinement process often involves continued training ( Dai et al., 2023 ) on highly curated and/or aesthetically superior datasets to eliminate structural artifacts and enhance fine-grained details. Furthermore, to bridge the gap between raw generative capability and complex user intent, researchers integrate human preference alignment and reinforcement learning methods ( Croitoru et al., 2025 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Na et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) . By directly optimizing for human-based reward signals, these advanced alignment strategies enhance structural coherence, aesthetic appeal, and strict prompt fidelity. Usually, the fine-tuning process operates on a massive data scale of its own. Although foundational models have already undergone rigorous pre-training on web-scale datasets, specialized datasets utilized during the fine-tuning phase remain exceptionally large ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . In this work, we show that the size of these datasets can be substantially reduced through a representative selection of samples from the original set. Figure 1: Overview of EigDiff (eigen-guided data selection). Preference image pairs are CLIP-encoded into embeddings, on which PCA yields the principal (eigen) components. Each pair is scored by its projection onto these directions ( 𝐰 ⋅ 𝐱 ⊤ \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}^{\top} for SFT, 𝐰 ⋅ ( 𝐱 − 𝐲 ) ⊤ \mathbf{w}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^{\top} for DPO). Per component, Stage 1 deterministically selects the exemplars (highest score). The figure illustrates the near to far spread. Stage 2 stratifies the full remaining score range via diversity quantiles. Best viewed in color. Despite the remarkable generative capabilities of diffusion models, the inherent latency of their iterative reverse process represents a significant drawback. Consequently, another important research direction has been the aggressive optimization of the inference phase, targeting a drastic reduction in the number of denoising steps required to generate an image ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) . The most popular methods to achieve this kind of accelerations are based on knowledge distillation ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . In such methods, a pre-trained student model is usually trained to predict the output of the teacher model over much larger denoising intervals. The resulting student is able to bypass a large portion, or even the entirety, of the intermediate denoising steps, enabling few-step or single-step image generation, while almost preserving the visual fidelity of the original model. Despite these optimizations achieved during inference, there are only a few works ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025b ) that tackle training efficiency. However, these methods either require a manual selection ( Dai et al., 2023 ) of the most representative samples, or are tested only on labeled datasets because the selection process is individually performed for each class ( Li et al., 2025a ) . This class-specific selection limits their applicability in real-world setups, like text-to-image generation. In contrast, we propose a fully-automated selection method and we show that it performs well on text-to-image synthesis. In this work, we focus on reducing the computational overhead of fine-tuning diffusion models by selecting a diverse subset of exemplar images from the training data, as illustrated in Figure 1 . We take inspiration from the seminal works of ( Sirovich and Kirby, 1987 ) and ( Pentland et al., 1994 ) , who apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract eigenfaces, i.e. a basis set of images that captures the greatest variance within a dataset of faces. However, the method is not robust to high data variations, e.g. natural images, as it is sensitive to affine transformations. To mitigate this problem, we propose to apply PCA in the CLIP latent space, to obtain a set of eigenvectors. We then use cosine similarity to retrieve the images that best align with the eigenvectors, ensuring that our subset spans the broad variations of the original data. However, selecting only the highest-aligning images fails to capture the internal diversity along each principal component. Therefore, we complement these initial exemplars using a stratified sampling strategy, selecting additional images that represent varying degrees of alignment to each component. Both dataset distillation steps are carried out with a focus on training budget, aiming to reduce the overall training time. We conduct experiments on four datasets (Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPDv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , Rapidata ( Christodoulou and Kuhlmann-Jørgensen, 2024 ) , ROCO Radiology ( Pelka et al., 2018 ) ), using two different diffusion models (Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and PixArt- α \alpha ( Chen et al., 2024 ) ). We consider two training setups, preference optimization and domain adaptation. Specifically, we verify the compatibility of our selection process with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , as well as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Our results show that our dataset distillation method based on eigenvectors produces similar performance levels, while reducing training time by several folds (between 5.86 × 5.86\times and 13.95 × 13.95\times ). In summary, our contribution is twofold: • We introduce EigDiff, a dataset distillation method that significantly reduces the computational overhead of fine-tuning diffusion model by selecting representative samples from the training set based on eigenvectors. • We verify the effectiveness and efficiency of EigDiff on different datasets, diffusion models, and fine-tuning strategies.

sections.heading: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.text: Diffusion models. Although diffusion models have been introduced a while ago in ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) , it is only through the more recent denoising probabilistic diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and their score-based counterparts ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021b ) that they have established themselves as the new paradigm for generative image modeling ( Croitoru et al., 2023 ) . Their recognition stemmed from greatly surpassing generative adversarial networks ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) , the previous leading paradigm, on both image fidelity and diversity ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . The scalability of diffusion models has been enabled through subsequent works ( Bao et al., 2023 ; Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Latent diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) reduced computational cost by operating in the compressed latent space of a pretrained autoencoder. ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) refined the noise schedule, while ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) and ( Bao et al., 2023 ) leveraged more efficient architectures. Later, ( Song et al., 2023 ) proposed a new type of diffusion models (called consistency models) that require only a few iterations. Nevertheless, all of these methods implicitly assume the availability of very large training corpora, a constraint we aim to mitigate in our work. Time step distillation. One of the main drawbacks of diffusion models is the large number of required sequential denoising steps, thus motivating a rich line of work on timestep distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Berthelot et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Chadebec et al., 2025 ) . One of the earlier pieces of work, namely Progressive Distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , aims to train a student model to match the output of two teacher steps in a single step, therefore halving the required number of steps. The most notable work in this direction is represented by Consistency Models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . These aim few-step generation by enforcing self-consistency along the entire probability flow ODE trajectory, i.e. directly learning the mapping between noisy and clean samples across multiple timestamps. This enables single-step generation, while multi-step refinement remains a valid option for improved quality. While time step distillation can significantly reduce inference time, the full dataset and the full model are still required during training, thereby limiting model fine-tuning with typical academic resources. Architecture distillation. Another adopted method for reducing the computational complexity and the total parameter count of diffusion models, while preserving the generation quality, is based on architectural distillation ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Moon et al., 2024 ) , i.e. compressing the architecture. Modern diffusion models rely on heavily over-parameterized U-Nets with attention mechanisms or transformer-based backbones. As a result, on the one hand, several works have investigated transferring knowledge from large teacher networks to lighter student architectures through feature matching or score alignment ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xiang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) , and, on the other hand, the models are pruned ( Fang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . ( Kim et al., 2024 ) proposed to reduce the blocks from the U-Net by employing three objectives: estimate the added noise during the forward pass (the usual objective of diffusion models), estimate the predicted noise of the teacher model, and match the feature maps between the teacher and student models. They managed to reduce the model size up to 51 % 51\% , while improving the latency by 43 % 43\% . ( Lee et al., 2024 ) scaled this approach to SDXL. ( Fang et al., 2023 ) presented a distillation method that offers a trade-off between efficiency and quality: sub-structures from the network are removed based on some importance scores computed using the gradient. Subsequent works focus on eliminating the redundancy of different parts from a diffusion model: layer-level distillation ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Gupta et al., 2024 ) , attention reduction ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , and even combining distillation and pruning ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . While effective, architecture distillation requires inference through the teacher model, which can represent a significant overhead during training. Our contribution is focused on dataset distillation, an orthogonal direction focused on reducing training time. Dataset distillation. Deep learning datasets often contain substantial redundancy, in which the contribution of many samples bring limited information gains. Several studies ( Cazenavette et al., 2022 ; Hondru and Ionescu, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Zhao et al., 2021 ) have shown that large neural networks can maintain strong performance even when trained on carefully selected subsets of the original data, although these have mainly been explored almost exclusively in the supervised classification regime. ( Dai et al., 2023 ) analyzed the impact of carefully selecting the training data for a text-to-image diffusion model and conclude that fine-tuning on a very small yet highly visually appealing set of images can substantially enhance generation quality. However, unlike our approach, after an initial automatic filtering (offensive content removal, aesthetic and CLIP-score filtering, OCR-based text filtering, image size and aspect ratio constraints, balancing categories such as portraits, landscapes, animals, food images, and finally some proprietary quality checks), they employed a manual labeling process in order to select candidate images. More recently, ( Li et al., 2025a ) proposed a scheme for pruning the training data. Embeddings of the data samples are initially obtained using the latent space of a pre-trained image classifier, and then, the most informative examples are selected according to a Gaussian-based model scoring criterion. After this, class weights are dynamically computed through distributionally robust optimization, using a pre-trained reference diffusion model. In contrast to existing methods, that either employ manual labeling ( Dai et al., 2023 ) or require a computationally intensive selection process involving deep neural models ( Li et al., 2025a ) , we propose a lightweight dataset distillation procedure that selects samples based on their similarity to a set of eigenvectors computed in a CLIP latent space.

sections.heading: 3 METHOD
sections.text: Motivation. EigDiff aims to identify a compressed training set of representative images that preserve (i) the dominant characteristics and (ii) the diversity of the entire dataset, while reducing data redundancy by as much as possible. To achieve these goals, we first extract EVA-CLIP ( Sun et al., 2023 ) embeddings from the images and apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to compute eigenvectors, which serve as a basis for reconstructing the embedding space. This approach is inspired by eigenfaces ( Pentland et al., 1994 ; Sirovich and Kirby, 1987 ) . However, because we operate on more complex visual domains, we cannot use raw eigenimages directly as training data for generative models. The eigenimages are highly sensitive to lighting variations and affine transformations, and they lack the high-frequency details specific to natural images, which are required for training high-quality generative models. To achieve (i), we select exemplars that encapsulate the dominant characteristics. We accomplish this by locating the latent vectors closest to each eigenvector within the embedding space and retaining its corresponding natural image. To achieve the second goal (ii), we propose to select additional samples using a stratified sampling approach, where the stratification is applied via similarity bins computed w.r.t. the eigenvectors. Selecting images from different similarity bins ensures a broad diversity among the select samples. Data preprocessing. We evaluate our method under two training paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). For SFT setup, the dataset comprises N N image-text pairs, D raw = { ( I i , c i ) } i = 1 N D_{\text{raw}}=\{(I_{i},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , where I i ∈ ℝ H × W × C I_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} represents an image of resolution H × W H\times W with C C channels, and c i c_{i} is a corresponding text prompt. For the DPO setup, the dataset is a collection of N N triplets, D raw = { ( I i w , I i l , c i ) } i = 1 N D_{\text{raw}}=\{(I_{i}^{w},I_{i}^{l},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , where I i w , I i l ∈ ℝ H × W × C I_{i}^{w},I_{i}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} denote the chosen (winning) and rejected (losing) images, respectively, both generated from the same prompt c i c_{i} . Let g : ℝ H × W × C → ℝ d g:\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a frozen image encoder that projects the images into a d d -dimensional space. In our case, the encoder is EVA-CLIP ( Sun et al., 2023 ) . In the preference optimization setup, we obtain L 2 L_{2} -normalized embeddings for the chosen and rejected images as x i w = g ⁡ ( I i w ) ∥ g ⁡ ( I i w ) ∥ x_{i}^{w}=\frac{g(I_{i}^{w})}{\lVert g(I_{i}^{w})\rVert} and x i l = g ⁡ ( I i l ) ∥ g ⁡ ( I i l ) ∥ x_{i}^{l}=\frac{g(I_{i}^{l})}{\lVert g(I_{i}^{l})\rVert} . Stacking these representations, we obtain the chosen and rejected embedding matrices, X w = [ x 1 w , … , x N w ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ N × d X^{w}=[x_{1}^{w},\dots,x_{N}^{w}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and X l = [ x 1 l , … , x N l ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ N × d X^{l}=[x_{1}^{l},\dots,x_{N}^{l}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} , respectively. sections.heading: 4.1 Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate EigDiff on one medical text-to-image dataset, ROCO Radiology ( Pelka et al., 2018 ) , alongside three text-to-image preference datasets: Pick-a-Pic v1 ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPDv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , and Rapidata ( Christodoulou and Kuhlmann-Jørgensen, 2024 ) . For all preference datasets, we first filter out the non-decision samples. To manage training size, we randomly subsample Pick-a-Pic v1 and HPDv2 to 100,000 100,000 training examples each, while retaining their original test sets of 500 500 and 400 400 prompts, respectively. Finally, from Rapidata, we utilize the human style preference split, allocating 45,030 45,030 pairs for training and 75 75 unique prompts for testing. ROCO Radiology ( Pelka et al., 2018 ) consists of pairs of medical images and captions, and it serves as an out-of-domain dataset for our selected generators. We apply two data filtering operations: retaining only the training samples with an aspect ratio between 0.7 0.7 and 1.35 1.35 and discarding samples with captions shorter than 6 words. Consequently, we remain with 42,050 42,050 preference pairs for training, and we utilize 500 500 prompts for testing.

sections.heading: 4.2 Training Setup
sections.text: Baselines. We compare our approach against seven baselines. The first baseline consists of the pre-trained models, Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) (SD1.5) and PixArt- α \alpha -XL-2 ( Chen et al., 2024 ) (PixArt- α \alpha ). The second is a full-scale fine-tuning on the entire datasets, representing a performance target that our method aims to match. Finally, we compare against a random selection variant, which keeps the exact same number of training samples as our method, but selects them randomly. In addition, we compare against four data selection methods: Greedy K-Center ( Gonzalez, 1985 ) , Stochastic-Greedy Facility Location ( Mirzasoleiman et al., 2015 ) , K-Means++ ( Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007 ) , and SemDeDup ( Abbas et al., 2023 ) . They follow the same configuration and budget ( n 1 + n 2 n_{1}+n_{2} ) as our approach. In the case of RapiData, methods such as K-Center, K-Means++ and SemDeDup retain all 4,888 unique samples, thus we train them for 2,444 steps with SD1.5, and 1,222 steps with PixArt- α \alpha . Hyperparameters. For both backbones, we employ AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , weight decay equal to 10 − 2 10^{-2} , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , with maximum gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 . We use a training batch size of 6 6 for SD1.5 and a batch size of 4 4 for PixArt- α \alpha . We set the learning rate to 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The learning rate schedule is constant and it has a warm-up phase. We use the classifier-free guidance with 20 % 20\% empty prompts. In order to reduce the computational complexity, we train the models using LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . For our LoRA configuration, we use a rank of 16 16 , α = 16 \alpha=16 , and dropout 0.01 0.01 . The LoRA layers are applied on the query, key, value and output projections layers, resulting in PixArt- α \alpha having 1.33 % 1.33\% trainable parameters and SD1.5 0.37 % 0.37\% . On Pick-a-Pic, HPDv2, and Rapidata, we train SD1.5 for 3 3 epochs, and PixArt- α \alpha for 1 1 epoch. On ROCO Radiology, we fine-tune both models for 8 8 epochs. In the DPO setup, we set β = 2000 \beta=2000 for SD1.5 and β = 5000 \beta=5000 for PixArt- α \alpha . At inference time, we use 50 50 denoising steps with classifier-free guidance of scale 7.5 7.5 for SD1.5, and 20 20 denoising steps with 4.5 4.5 scale for PixArt- α \alpha . In Table 1 , we detail the hyperparameters specific to EigDiff. Specifically, for each dataset, we present the budget of samples for the first stage n 1 n_{1} , the ratio of samples for the second stage δ = n 2 n 1 \delta=\frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} , the number of intervals B B employed in second stage, and the variance thresholds ( τ 1 , τ 2 ) (\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) . sections.text: We present a qualitative analysis over DPO and SFT with all the baselines and our method in Figures 3 and 4 , respectively. DPO visualization. In the first column of Figure 3 , EigDiff aligns most closely with the prompt, whereas the full-scale model fails to generate the starry sky. Additionally, the random and pre-trained variants depict a Pop Mart figure with short hair, but fail to produce a high-quality macaroon. In the second column, EigDiff again achieves the best result, being the only strategy capable of generating a high-quality close-up of a sheep crossing the street with both a car and a man appropriately focused on the scene. The third and fourth columns similarly favor EigDiff, which produces the most prompt-aligned, high-quality images. Likewise, in the fifth column, EigDiff is the only method that avoids noticeable hallucinations. The pre-trained variant, for example, lacks arms and exhibits an awkward head shape and sleeping posture. Finally, in the last column, EigDiff produces the most recognizable psychedelic duck, with a well-defined side profile and vibrant, coherent coloration. In contrast, the pre-trained and full-scale variants fail to preserve the duck’s structure, while the random selection generates a plausible frontal-view duck wearing glasses, but with lower overall definition and visual quality. sections.heading: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.text: In this paper, we presented EigDiff, a data-selection pipeline that embeds preference pairs with a frozen CLIP-based encoder, fits a PCA subspace on the preferred images, scores each pair by its signed alignment with the principal directions, and selects a compact subset via a two-stage, variance-proportional, stratified procedure. We performed experiments with two diffusion backbones (SD1.5 and PixArt- α \alpha ), two fine-tuning regimes (DPO and SFT), and four datasets spanning natural and medical preference pairs with prompts. Our eigen selection method generally matches or exceeds the full-scale fine-tuning scores and surpasses all random experiments (at equal budget), while reducing GPU-minutes between 5.87 × 5.87\times and 13.95 × 13.95\times through subset selection. Against four selection baselines with an identical configuration, EigDiff is best or second-best in 12 of 14 cases, at a selection cost between 3.1 × 3.1\times and 1607 × 1607\times lower. Our ablations show that the deterministic exemplars carry the dominant preference signal, while the stratified secondary directions supply non-redundant diversity. They also confirm that our variance-proportional budgeting has an important role in linking the first stage and the quantile-based second stage. The selection cost is a single PCA over cached embeddings, making the method a cheap, model-agnostic preprocessing step for preference-based diffusion fine-tuning. Limitations include reliance on the embedding geometry of the encoder.

Andrei Jarca, Vlad Hondru, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Radu Tudor Ionescu University of Bucharest, Romania Corresponding author: raducu.ionescu@gmail.com Abstract Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14 × 14\times and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607 × 1607\times , with marginal performance differences. 1 INTRODUCTION Diffusion models ( Croitoru et al., 2023 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2021a ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) have consistently demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image synthesis in recent years. Some of the recent developments of diffusion models have focused on improving the quality of the generated samples. This is often achieved by a specialized post-training or fine-tuning phase ( Zhang et al., 2024c ; Luo et al., 2025 ) designed to improve the base models toward better visual and semantic results. This refinement process often involves continued training ( Dai et al., 2023 ) on highly curated and/or aesthetically superior datasets to eliminate structural artifacts and enhance fine-grained details. Furthermore, to bridge the gap between raw generative capability and complex user intent, researchers integrate human preference alignment and reinforcement learning methods ( Croitoru et al., 2025 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Na et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) . By directly optimizing for human-based reward signals, these advanced alignment strategies enhance structural coherence, aesthetic appeal, and strict prompt fidelity. Usually, the fine-tuning process operates on a massive data scale of its own. Although foundational models have already undergone rigorous pre-training on web-scale datasets, specialized datasets utilized during the fine-tuning phase remain exceptionally large ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . In this work, we show that the size of these datasets can be substantially reduced through a representative selection of samples from the original set. Figure 1: Overview of EigDiff (eigen-guided data selection). Preference image pairs are CLIP-encoded into embeddings, on which PCA yields the principal (eigen) components. Each pair is scored by its projection onto these directions ( 𝐰 ⋅ 𝐱 ⊤ \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}^{\top} for SFT, 𝐰 ⋅ ( 𝐱 − 𝐲 ) ⊤ \mathbf{w}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^{\top} for DPO). Per component, Stage 1 deterministically selects the exemplars (highest score). The figure illustrates the near to far spread. Stage 2 stratifies the full remaining score range via diversity quantiles. Best viewed in color. Despite the remarkable generative capabilities of diffusion models, the inherent latency of their iterative reverse process represents a significant drawback. Consequently, another important research direction has been the aggressive optimization of the inference phase, targeting a drastic reduction in the number of denoising steps required to generate an image ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) . The most popular methods to achieve this kind of accelerations are based on knowledge distillation ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) . In such methods, a pre-trained student model is usually trained to predict the output of the teacher model over much larger denoising intervals. The resulting student is able to bypass a large portion, or even the entirety, of the intermediate denoising steps, enabling few-step or single-step image generation, while almost preserving the visual fidelity of the original model. Despite these optimizations achieved during inference, there are only a few works ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025b ) that tackle training efficiency. However, these methods either require a manual selection ( Dai et al., 2023 ) of the most representative samples, or are tested only on labeled datasets because the selection process is individually performed for each class ( Li et al., 2025a ) . This class-specific selection limits their applicability in real-world setups, like text-to-image generation. In contrast, we propose a fully-automated selection method and we show that it performs well on text-to-image synthesis. In this work, we focus on reducing the computational overhead of fine-tuning diffusion models by selecting a diverse subset of exemplar images from the training data, as illustrated in Figure 1 . We take inspiration from the seminal works of ( Sirovich and Kirby, 1987 ) and ( Pentland et al., 1994 ) , who apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract eigenfaces, i.e. a basis set of images that captures the greatest variance within a dataset of faces. However, the method is not robust to high data variations, e.g. natural images, as it is sensitive to affine transformations. To mitigate this problem, we propose to apply PCA in the CLIP latent space, to obtain a set of eigenvectors. We then use cosine similarity to retrieve the images that best align with the eigenvectors, ensuring that our subset spans the broad variations of the original data. However, selecting only the highest-aligning images fails to capture the internal diversity along each principal component. Therefore, we complement these initial exemplars using a stratified sampling strategy, selecting additional images that represent varying degrees of alignment to each component. Both dataset distillation steps are carried out with a focus on training budget, aiming to reduce the overall training time. We conduct experiments on four datasets (Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPDv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , Rapidata ( Christodoulou and Kuhlmann-Jørgensen, 2024 ) , ROCO Radiology ( Pelka et al., 2018 ) ), using two different diffusion models (Stable Diffusion 1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and PixArt- α \alpha ( Chen et al., 2024 ) ). We consider two training setups, preference optimization and domain adaptation. Specifically, we verify the compatibility of our selection process with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , as well as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Our results show that our dataset distillation method based on eigenvectors produces similar performance levels, while reducing training time by several folds (between 5.86 × 5.86\times and 13.95 × 13.95\times ). In summary, our contribution is twofold: • We introduce EigDiff, a dataset distillation method that significantly reduces the computational overhead of fine-tuning diffusion model by selecting representative samples from the training set based on eigenvectors. • We verify the effectiveness and efficiency of EigDiff on different datasets, diffusion models, and fine-tuning strategies. 2 RELATED WORK Diffusion models. Although diffusion models have been introduced a while ago in ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) , it is only through the more recent denoising probabilistic diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and their score-based counterparts ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021b ) that they have established themselves as the new paradigm for generative image modeling ( Croitoru et al., 2023 ) . Their recognition stemmed from greatly surpassing generative adversarial networks ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) , the previous leading paradigm, on both image fidelity and diversity ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . The scalability of diffusion models has been enabled through subsequent works ( Bao et al., 2023 ; Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Latent diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) reduced computational cost by operating in the compressed latent space of a pretrained autoencoder. ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) refined the noise schedule, while ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) and ( Bao et al., 2023 ) leveraged more efficient architectures. Later, ( Song et al., 2023 ) proposed a new type of diffusion models (called consistency models) that require only a few iterations. Nevertheless, all of these methods implicitly assume the availability of very large training corpora, a constraint we aim to mitigate in our work. Time step distillation. One of the main drawbacks of diffusion models is the large number of required sequential denoising steps, thus motivating a rich line of work on timestep distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Berthelot et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Chadebec et al., 2025 ) . One of the earlier pieces of work, namely Progressive Distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , aims to train a student model to match the output of two teacher steps in a single step, therefore halving the required number of steps. The most notable work in this direction is represented by Consistency Models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . These aim few-step generation by enforcing self-consistency along the entire probability flow ODE trajectory, i.e. directly learning the mapping between noisy and clean samples across multiple timestamps. This enables single-step generation, while multi-step refinement remains a valid option for improved quality. While time step distillation can significantly reduce inference time, the full dataset and the full model are still required during training, thereby limiting model fine-tuning with typical academic resources. Architecture distillation. Another adopted method for reducing the computational complexity and the total parameter count of diffusion models, while preserving the generation quality, is based on architectural distillation ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Moon et al., 2024 ) , i.e. compressing the architecture. Modern diffusion models rely on heavily over-parameterized U-Nets with attention mechanisms or transformer-based backbones. As a result, on the one hand, several works have investigated transferring knowledge from large teacher networks to lighter student architectures through feature matching or score alignment ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xiang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) , and, on the other hand, the models are pruned ( Fang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . ( Kim et al., 2024 ) proposed to reduce the blocks from the U-Net by employing three objectives: estimate the added noise during the forward pass (the usual objective of diffusion models), estimate the predicted noise of the teacher model, and match the feature maps between the teacher and student models. They managed to reduce the model size up to 51 % 51\% , while improving the latency by 43 % 43\% . ( Lee et al., 2024 ) scaled this approach to SDXL. ( Fang et al., 2023 ) presented a distillation method that offers a trade-off between efficiency and quality: sub-structures from the network are removed based on some importance scores computed using the gradient. Subsequent works focus on eliminating the redundancy of different parts from a diffusion model: layer-level distillation ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Gupta et al., 2024 ) , attention reduction ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , and even combining distillation and pruning ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . While effective, architecture distillation requires inference through the teacher model, which can represent a significant overhead during training. Our contribution is focused on dataset distillation, an orthogonal direction focused on reducing training time. Dataset distillation. Deep learning datasets often contain substantial redundancy, in which the contribution of many samples bring limited information gains. Several studies ( Cazenavette et al., 2022 ; Hondru and Ionescu, 2025 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Zhao et al., 2021 ) have shown that large neural networks can maintain strong performance even when trained on carefully selected subsets of the original data, although these have mainly been explored almost exclusively in the supervised classification regime. ( Dai et al., 2023 ) analyzed the impact of carefully selecting the training data for a text-to-image diffusion model and conclude that fine-tuning on a very small yet highly visually appealing set of images can substantially enhance generation quality. However, unlike our approach, after an initial automatic filtering (offensive content removal, aesthetic and CLIP-score filtering, OCR-based text filtering, image size and aspect ratio constraints, balancing categories such as portraits, landscapes, animals, food images, and finally some proprietary quality checks), they employed a manual labeling process in order to select candidate images. More recently, ( Li et al., 2025a ) proposed a scheme for pruning the training data. Embeddings of the data samples are initially obtained using the latent space of a pre-trained image classifier, and then, the most informative examples are selected according to a Gaussian-based model scoring criterion. After this, class weights are dynamically computed through distributionally robust optimization, using a pre-trained reference diffusion model. In contrast to existing methods, that either employ manual labeling ( Dai et al., 2023 ) or require a computationally intensive selection process involving deep neural models ( Li et al., 2025a ) , we propose a lightweight dataset distillation procedure that selects samples based on their similarity to a set of eigenvectors computed in a CLIP latent space. 3 METHOD Motivation. EigDiff aims to identify a compressed training set of representative images that preserve (i) the dominant characteristics and (ii) the diversity of the entire dataset, while reducing data redundancy by as much as possible. To achieve these goals, we first extract EVA-CLIP ( Sun et al., 2023 ) embeddings from the images and apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to compute eigenvectors, which serve as a basis for reconstructing the embedding space. This approach is inspired by eigenfaces ( Pentland et al., 1994 ; Sirovich and Kirby, 1987 ) . However, because we operate on more complex visual domains, we cannot use raw eigenimages directly as training data for generative models. The eigenimages are highly sensitive to lighting variations and affine transformations, and they lack the high-frequency details specific to natural images, which are required for training high-quality generative models. To achieve (i), we select exemplars that encapsulate the dominant characteristics. We accomplish this by locating the latent vectors closest to each eigenvector within the embedding space and retaining its corresponding natural image. To achieve the second goal (ii), we propose to select additional samples using a stratified sampling approach, where the stratification is applied via similarity bins computed w.r.t. the eigenvectors. Selecting images from different similarity bins ensures a broad diversity among the select samples. Data preprocessing.
